result.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers say clearly that a desktop licence usually does not cover web use, and both send the user to the designer, the foundry or the licence without claiming to know this font's terms. B is better because it warns that the team's laptops will show the installed font and hide what visitors see, and because it notes that the licence may forbid converting to WOFF2; A simply recommends converting the files without that check. B's code section after the licence is confirmed is longer than needed, and neither answer says outright that the fallback will not match the brand font. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers correctly say not to upload the files yet and send the user to the designer or foundry to confirm web rights, without claiming to know the terms. A is better because it leaves the brand font out of the interim stack and warns that the team's laptops will show the locally installed font, so they won't see what visitors see. B puts "Marlowe Grotesk" first in its interim stack, which causes exactly that problem; its route to a licensed webfont is tighter, and its free OFL grotesk options are useful.
